claim: State may be a string, JSON object, or array; TypeSafe recommends an object with descriptive field names for most requests.
quote: Use an object for most requests so each part of the state has a descriptive name and its relationships remain clear. A string is suitable when the use case is simple and requires only one piece of text.
why: Directly answers format question and implies key names carry meaning.

claim: TypeSafe's own test asked 13 questions 5 times both batched and one-per-request and found no batching effect; most answers were identical across repeats (std dev 0.0), two nouls showed small run-to-run noise.
quote: Choices, scores, and six of the eight nouls come back identical across the 5 repeats: std dev exactly 0.0 under both batching strategies
why: Determinism and batching independence, with evidence that some sampling noise exists.

claim: Context limit is 64k tokens per request total, and 32k tokens for the state plus the single longest question; state is ingested once.
quote: Context length | 64k tokens per request; 32k tokens for `state` plus the longest question
why: Hard cap for gather.py state sizing.

claim: TypeSafe says accuracy falls as state grows with irrelevant content (context rot); filter in code and send only fields the question needs.
quote: Accuracy falls as the state grows with content unrelated to the decision. Unrelated detail acts as a distractor, and a large state makes it harder to tell which part of the input produced a wrong answer.

claim: Jev-1.13 is unreliable at counting, arithmetic, numeric precision, and date comparison; TypeSafe says keep math and date logic in code.
quote: `jev-1.13` reads dates as text, not as ordered quantities. Asking which of two dates comes first, how far apart they are, or whether one falls inside a window is unreliable.
why: Capability limits: arithmetic and date comparison (e.g. card publish dates).

claim: Choice confidence is (p_max - 1/n)/(1 - 1/n), i.e. clamp((n*max(p)-1)/(n-1)); Score confidence uses a different spread-based formula; Noul returns no confidence (use |2p-1|).
quote: For a Choice with $n$ options, where $p_{\max}$ is the probability of the selected option: $$ \text{confidence} = \frac{p_{\max} - \frac{1}{n}}{1 - \frac{1}{n}} $$
why: Confirms claimed Choice formula and corrects it for Score.

claim: The fractional Score value is the probability-weighted mean of level indices (0..n-1) and should not be interpolated as a magnitude.
quote: The score is a probability-weighted mean of the level numbers. In the third and fourth examples, probability is split between levels 1 and 2. More weight on level 2 raises the score.
why: How score fraction is computed; pair with jaggedness warning on weak numeric calibration of levels.

claim: JevAdvBench found identical requests change the returned Score value for 38.5% of Score questions, though the decision-flip noise floor is only 1.0%.
quote: Sending an identical request twice changes the returned Score value for 38.5% of Score questions, which inflates the clean error under exact matching to 9.98% (2.2% within a quarter level)
why: Run-to-run variance; contradicts 'fully deterministic' assumption; preprint not peer reviewed yet.

claim: JevAdvBench: paraphrasing the question moves decisions at most 1.2pp over re-run noise, out-of-schema fields are never billed or seen, but one appended observer opinion in state flips 12.1% of decisions.
quote: On jev-1.13.0, rewording stays within 1.2 percentage points of the re-run baseline, and fields outside the schema never reach the model. In contrast, one unverified opinion appended to the state flips 12.1% of decisions
why: State content (argued text) matters far more than question wording; extra request keys are dropped.

claim: CMU judge study: Jev changed no decision across 96 repeated requests, 4 of 48 rubric paraphrases changed decisions, candidate-order reversal flipped 95 of 1,850 pairs, and larger gaps vs a frontier judge appear on derivation-checking.
quote: JEV changes no decision across 96 repeated requests but four of 48 paraphrases, as many as any judge
why: Determinism plus paraphrase and type sensitivity; preprint.

claim: Independent tester found Jev best on short input with crisp labels; accuracy and confidence fall together on longer input and business-logic-heavy questions, and mention-vs-value questions swung 0.5 between runs.
quote: The longer the input and the fuzzier the labels, or the more business logic the question carries, the more its accuracy and its confidence fall together. On a whole-document read it is worse than the small model we run today, and no prompt fixed that.
why: Length effect and variance from 16k-call test.

claim: On Norwegian text Jev's tokenizer gives ~2.06 chars/token, so 32k-token state cap is about 64k characters; Jev still found a key demand at the end of a twelve-page document.
quote: Jev's tokenizer gets about 2.06 characters per token on Norwegian. The limit for the state is 32k tokens, so that is roughly 64,000 characters of Norwegian and not the 120,000 you would guess from English.
why: Languages and length/position (end-of-document content found); single small test.

claim: English is the primary training language; other languages including CJK are handled with lower accuracy.
quote: English is the primary training language and where accuracy is currently best. Other languages, including CJK scripts, are handled but not equally well; test on your own content before relying on Jev for a non-English workload

claim: The question map key is not sent to the model, so naming of question ids does not affect inference (unlike state field names).
quote: A key you choose. The matching Answer is returned under this same id. The key is not sent to the underlying model and is not used in inference.
why: Which names matter: question keys don't; criteria option keys and state keys likely do.

claim: TypeSafe (quoted on HN) says Jev lacks deep knowledge of niche domains and context must be supplied in state.
quote: Jev doesn't have deep knowledge of niche domains, but you can supply context to help it decide.
why: World knowledge limits; secondhand quote, not verified on docs.

claim: Launch post: Jev uses a new architecture and a parallel sampler; high-cardinality choices use a 2-stage score-independently-then-choose system.
quote: For the higher cardinality choices, we do a 2 stage-system of scoring independently then making an explicit choice, hence the occassional slowdown.
why: Only architecture hint found; relevant to many-option Choices.
